cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: A fraud filter needs a compact way to combine purchase amount and an abroad flag. A weighted score lets the same recipe process every transaction. First we must learn to read that recipe.
cards.explain: A scalar is one number. A vector is an ordered list. A matrix is a table of numbers. A feature is a measured input; a label is the answer we hope to predict. Here y=1 and y=0 name classes, not good and bad. A hat means an estimate: y is truth, while ŷ is the predicted class. The subscript i names a sample (row); j names a feature (column).
cards.teach: Each row of X describes one sample. Each column has one consistent meaning. A weight says how strongly its feature affects a score. The special input x₀=1 makes a fixed starting score possible. That input is the bias feature; w₀ is its weight (the intercept). A score is not yet a probability.

cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: A priority flag on a phone notification may make it seem important, but the flag alone cannot tell us its probability of truly needing attention. We must combine how common important notifications are with how often each kind gets flagged. Odds make that update a multiplication.
cards.explain: A probability is the fraction of a group having a property. P(A|B) reads “probability of A among cases where B is true.” The bar changes the group we count within. P(A|B) usually differs from P(B|A). A complement is “not A,” so its probability is 1−P(A). In HW6 phishing and legitimate exhaust the possibilities. A joint probability P(A,B) counts both properties together.
cards.source: Day 11 pp. 5–6, 15; HW6 p. 2 (probability prerequisites unpacked here)
cards.teach: Fresh teaching example, not course data: imagine 100 notifications, 20 important and 80 routine. A priority flag appears on 10 important and 20 routine notifications. Among the 30 flagged notifications, 10 are important. Counting within this new group is Bayes’ rule.

cards.explain: Connection to the previous lesson: a weighted score can be any real number; probability and odds give us the language needed to interpret its eventual output. Probability uses total cases in the denominator; odds uses opposite-class cases. Next we take a logarithm of odds so multiplicative evidence can become an additive score.
cards.source: Day 11 pp. 5–6, 15; HW6 p. 2 (probability prerequisites unpacked here)
cards.math: For this teaching example, prior odds=20/80=1/4. The flag likelihood ratio is (10/20)/(20/80)=(1/2)/(1/4)=2. Posterior odds=2×1/4=1/2. Convert to probability: (1/2)/(1+1/2)=(1/2)/(3/2)=1/3. Count check: 10/(10+20)=1/3. “Half of important notifications are flagged” is not “half of flagged notifications are important.” Without a flag, counts are 10 important and 60 routine: odds=1/6 and probability=1/7.

cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: A straight regression line can predict values below zero or above one. For a fraud probability that is impossible. Logistic regression keeps a simple weighted score, then bends it into the probability range. Like a dimmer approaching full brightness, its output saturates instead of growing forever.
cards.explain: An exponential eᶻ is always positive; e≈2.71828. Multiplication of exponentials adds exponents: eᵃeᵇ=eᵃ⁺ᵇ. The natural log ln reverses an exponential: ln(eᶻ)=z and e^(ln a)=a for a>0. ln(ab)=ln a+ln b. A log can be negative: ln(1/2)=−ln 2. “Linear in features” includes the bias here, so z=w₀+w₁x₁+… .
cards.teach: The model assumes log odds equals the weighted score. Score zero means odds one, hence probability one half. Positive scores favor class one; negative scores favor class zero. The curve gets flatter near zero and one. More confidence does not require changing the predicted class.

cards.prompt: Walk through a small example before testing yourself.
cards.answer: Worked example: follow each line below.
cards.explain: Connection to the previous lesson: evidence multiplied odds; taking logs turns those multiplications into additions, which a weighted score can represent. A probability estimate and a class prediction are different outputs. A weight’s units are per input unit: HW6 amount is hundreds of dollars. Next we score how good the probabilities are.
cards.math:
Teaching example: z=ln 3 gives odds e^(ln 3)=3 and p=3/(1+3)=3/4. Add a weight ln 2 from a one-unit feature increase: odds become 3×2=6 and probability becomes 6/7, not 2×3/4. For a second teaching score z=−ln 3, the odds are 1/3 and p=(1/3)/(4/3)=1/4. Its class-0 probability is 3/4.

A probability threshold is a separate decision rule. HW6 uses p≥0.5, so z≥0 predicts class 1. Day 12 p.20 prints a strict >0 rule; exactly at zero we follow HW6’s ≥ convention.

cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: Two weather apps both predict rain. One assigns rain 51%, the other 99%. A correct/incorrect mark treats them equally, but their probabilities make different claims. Cross-entropy judges the probability assigned to what actually happened, and strongly penalizes confident mistakes.
cards.explain: First identify the true label y. Write p for predicted class-1 probability, and q for predicted probability of the true class. If y=1, q=p; if y=0, q=1−p. Σ means “add one term for each sample.” A product Π multiplies them. A mean is a sum divided by the number of terms n. ln is increasing, so bigger q gives bigger ln q; a minus sign reverses that order. For the course likelihood product, labels are modeled independently across samples once inputs and weights are fixed, allowing their probabilities to multiply.
cards.teach: A true-class probability near one contributes almost zero loss. A tiny true-class probability contributes a large positive loss. “Most correctly classified” in these lectures means highest true-class probability, even when several samples share the same correct/incorrect label.

Sum J≈1.415037 bits; mean L≈0.707519 bits. In nats, the sum is ln 2+ln(4/3)=ln(8/3)≈0.980829. The first sample is less correct, because 1/2<3/4.

cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: To improve a recipe, you need to know whether a little more of an ingredient helps or hurts. A derivative measures that local change. A gradient does the same for all weights, so we can improve a model without guessing every possible recipe.
cards.explain: A function maps inputs to an output. A derivative f′(a) measures the limiting change in output per unit input near a. A tangent is the line matching the local slope. A partial derivative changes one coordinate while freezing the rest. ∇ (“nabla”) collects those partials in a column. A norm measures vector length: ||[a,b]||₂=√(a²+b²).
cards.teach: Positive slope means moving right increases output locally; negative slope means moving right decreases it. The gradient points toward fastest local increase, so descent moves against it. Zero derivative means stationary: it could be a minimum, maximum, or flat non-extremum. The optimization slides use minimum-oriented shorthand; zero slope alone is not a general minimum test.

cards.prompt: Walk through a small example before testing yourself.
cards.answer: Worked example: follow each line below.
cards.explain: Connection to the previous lesson: loss is a function of the weights, and slopes tell us how that function changes when a weight moves. The gradient is a vector of slopes, not a new weight vector. Compute every component at the old weights. Next the chain rule makes cross-entropy training simple.
cards.math: Teaching example: f(w)=w₀²+3w₁² at w=[1,−1]. Partial slopes are 2 and −6; gradient [2,−6] has length √(4+36)=√40. With step α=0.1, new vector=[1,−1]−0.1[2,−6]=[0.8,−0.4]. Old loss=1+3=4. New loss=0.8²+3(−0.4)²=0.64+0.48=1.12.

The gradient points toward fastest local increase, so descent moves against it. Zero derivative means stationary: it could be a minimum, maximum, or flat non-extremum. The optimization slides use minimum-oriented shorthand; zero slope alone is not a general minimum test.

cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: A nursery has survival labels for seedlings. It wants true outcomes to get higher probability overall. Gradient descent gives one coordinated adjustment from every seedling’s feedback, rather than fixing one case and forgetting the others.
cards.explain: Recall pᵢ=σ(xᵢ·w), yᵢ is 0 or 1, and J is a natural-log sum. The residual rᵢ=pᵢ−yᵢ is signed prediction error in probability. Xᵀ swaps rows and columns; multiplying it by residuals adds each feature’s error-weighted values. α (sometimes η in lecture demos) is a positive learning rate.

Samples can pull the same weights in opposing directions. A step can lower total loss while worsening individual cases.

cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: A coffee shop predicts drip, latte, or cold brew. A binary yes/no classifier cannot name all three in one output. We can assemble binary decisions, much as a tournament uses pairwise matches to pick a winner.
cards.explain: K is the number of classes. A pair is unordered: A vs B is the same classifier as B vs A. A vote is one classifier’s predicted class. A score is its confidence value. Binary logistic probabilities from separate models need not form a single probability distribution.
cards.teach: One vs rest (OvR) asks one question per class: “this class, or anything else?” Choose the largest score. One vs one (OvO) trains one classifier for each pair, using samples from those two classes, then chooses the class with the most pairwise votes in the course’s scheme.

cards.prompt: Walk through a small example before testing yourself.
cards.answer: Worked example: follow each line below.
cards.explain: Connection to the previous lesson: binary training makes one yes/no model; these strategies combine several such models. OvO uses each pair’s data. OvR uses the other classes as a combined negative group. Next we build one multiclass model rather than combining binary ones.
cards.math: Three drinks: OvR is drip/rest, latte/rest, cold-brew/rest → 3 models. OvO is drip/latte, drip/cold-brew, latte/cold-brew → 3 models. If drip wins the first two and latte the third, votes are [2,1,0]; choose drip. OvR probabilities 0.7,0.4,0.1 can sum to 1.2: choose the largest, but these are not a normalized class distribution.

cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: For a drink order, we want one probability for each possible drink and a total of one. Softmax converts class scores into that distribution. Imagine splitting a fixed pie among competing choices: increasing one share must take share from others.
cards.explain: Each class k gets weight vector wₖ and score zₖ=wₖ·x. Σⱼ adds over all classes j. exp(z) means eᶻ. arg max means “the index of the largest value,” not that value itself. The indicator 1(y=k) is one when its statement is true, zero otherwise.
cards.teach: Exponentiate scores to create positive strengths, then divide by their total. Larger scores get larger probabilities. Adding the same constant to all scores leaves the shares unchanged. Multiplying all scores by a constant generally changes confidence.

Normalize across classes within each sample, never down the sample column. Negative scores are allowed; negative probabilities are not. Next apply the chain to HW6 from a blank page.

cards.teach: Exponentiate scores to create positive strengths, then divide by their total. Larger scores get larger probabilities. Adding the same constant to all scores leaves the shares unchanged. Multiplying all scores by a constant generally changes confidence.
